Case Study

Discord

Discord DMs and Channels Enhancement

Role
UX/UI Designer · User Researcher · Illustrator
Type
Personal Project
Industry
Communication Services
Date
October 2025

Overview

The Challenge

Discord has grown from a gaming-first chat app into a daily communication tool for millions of communities, but its navigation patterns have not kept pace with how many users now juggle dozens of servers, channels, and DMs at once.

This project set out to improve how people move between servers, channels, and direct messages, with a focus on discovery, switching, and reducing the cognitive load of a crowded sidebar.

Background

As a long-time Discord user active across both gaming and professional communities, I noticed recurring friction in how the platform surfaces new servers and organizes existing ones, and used that as the starting point for a self-directed research and redesign project.

Problem Statement

How Might We

How might we help Discord users discover, organize, and switch between servers and conversations more efficiently, without disrupting the habits of people who already feel at home in the app?

Objectives & Goals

01

Make server discovery fast and intuitive across devices

02

Enable seamless switching between servers, channels, and DMs with minimal context loss

03

Surface and prioritize the user's most relevant chats and voice channels

04

Minimize cognitive load by collapsing or hiding low-priority content by default

05

Provide quick-access controls for frequently used conversations and servers

06

Improve scannability of channels and server lists so users can find conversations at a glance

Constraints

Designing Around Existing Habits

Any change had to work within Discord's already familiar interaction patterns for a large, habituated user base. As an unaffiliated personal project, every decision was validated against self run survey data only, not real platform analytics.

Design Process

My Approach

I ran this as a self-directed research and design project, moving from a broad survey of Discord users to targeted usability testing on a working prototype, validating navigation assumptions at each stage rather than relying on intuition alone.

Research

Business Challenges

Discord's growth has been driven by network effects between communities, which makes navigation friction especially costly: a user who can't find their way back to a server, or back into the right channel, is at risk of disengaging from that community entirely. Any redesign also had to respect that Discord's existing patterns are deeply learned habits for its most active users, so the goal was targeted improvement rather than wholesale reinvention.

User Research

Key Insights

Surveying Discord's target users, gamers and community members aged 16–40, revealed clear patterns in how people use and struggle with the platform.

86%
use Discord daily
100%
use text chat · 67% use voice chat · 33% use screen sharing
40%
can't live without text chats
43%
would like better server and channel navigation
100%
primarily use Discord on mobile or desktop/laptop
8%
find it difficult to navigate between servers and channels

User Research

User Personas

Through research I identified two primary user archetypes with distinct needs, mental models, and pain points, shaping the design decisions throughout the project.

User Testing

Testing the Mid-Fidelity Prototype

I ran moderated usability sessions on the mid-fidelity prototype with 7 participants who matched the target user profile, asking them to complete core tasks like joining a new server, finding a specific channel, and locating an old conversation. The sessions surfaced a few usability issues the wireframes alone hadn't revealed.

7
participants completed a moderated task-based session on the prototype
5 of 7
missed the Discover tab on their first attempt to join a new server
4 of 7
tried to drag and reorder pinned servers, which the prototype didn't support
3 of 7
did not realize the collapsed channel sidebar could expand
9.4 min
average time to complete all three core tasks, longer than the 6 minute target
6 of 7
rated the new layout easier to scan than the current Discord app despite the issues above
01

The Discover entry point was easy to miss

Most participants looked for new servers inside their existing server list rather than the separate Discover tab. The tab needed stronger visual weight and a clearer label before moving to high fidelity.

02

Pinned servers needed a clearer affordance

Several participants expected to reorder their pinned servers by dragging them, a behavior the mid-fidelity version never accounted for. This pointed to a small but real gap between the wireframe and how people actually expect lists to behave.

03

The collapsed sidebar hid more than it should have

The collapse icon alone wasn't a strong enough signal that channels were still there, just hidden. Participants assumed the channel list had disappeared entirely rather than collapsed, which changed how prominent that control needed to be.

Trade-offs

Alternatives Considered

01

Restructure the navigation, or refine it?

We considered a more dramatic restructure of the information architecture, but chose to refine the existing server, channel, and DM structure instead. Only 8% of surveyed users found current navigation difficult, so a full rebuild risked breaking habits for the comfortable majority.

02

Voice first, or text first?

We considered prioritizing voice channel features to match Discord's voice first identity, but chose text and DM improvements instead. The data showed heavier, more universal reliance on text: 100% of users relied on it and 40% called it indispensable, compared to 67% for voice.

03

Automatic prioritization, or manual control?

We considered automatically hiding low priority servers and channels based on usage, but chose manual collapse controls instead, so the platform isn't deciding what matters to a user on their behalf.
